Let $d,q\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$. For a parameter $\theta\in\Theta$, write $v_\theta(t,z):=v(t,z,\theta)$. The **parameterized ordinary differential equation** on $I$ is the initial-value problem

$$\dot z(t)=v_\theta(t,z(t)),\qquad z(s)=z_s,$$

where $s\in I$ and $z_s\in\mathbb R^d$. A trajectory on an interval $J\subseteq I$ containing $s$ is a differentiable function $z:J\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying both displayed conditions. Here $v_\theta$ is the state-velocity field.

It is a **parameterized neural ordinary differential equation**, or **neural ODE**, when $v_\theta(t,z)$ is specified by a neural network with input $(t,z)$ and $d$ outputs. Here a network is a fixed finite directed acyclic graph evaluated in an order in which every edge points to a later vertex: input vertices hold the coordinates of $(t,z)$, each other vertex applies a fixed scalar activation to an affine combination of earlier vertex values, and the output vertices use the identity activation. The weights and biases are specified functions of $\theta$ and may be shared or fixed. No particular depth, width, or hidden activation is prescribed; affine networks with no hidden vertices are allowed.

The general parameterized ODE remains defined for fields without such a network specification. This definition alone asserts neither solution existence beyond its stated interval nor numerical accuracy.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $x:(\alpha,\beta)\to\mathbb R^n$ solve a Picard-Lindelof ODE and suppose $\beta<\infty$. If there are $t_j\uparrow\beta$ for which $(t_j,x(t_j))$ lies in one compact subset $K$ of the open ODE domain, then $x$ extends to a solution beyond $\beta$. A solution whose graph has a sequence approaching a compact interior endpoint state extends past that endpoint. The reflected statement holds at a finite left endpoint.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and let
$F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth. For every base point $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ there are
$h>0$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $(t_0,x_0)$ such that each initial pair
$(s,y)\in W$ has a unique solution on $[s-h,s+h]$, and the resulting local
solution map is smooth in the initial time and initial state.

Let $F:D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and
$C^1$ in the state variable. Fix data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ and a compact time
interval $I=[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ on which the corresponding solutions through nearby
initial states all exist. Then the solution map

$$\Phi:I\times U_0\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad \Phi(t,y)=x(t;y),$$

is $C^1$ in the initial-state variable $y$ on some neighbourhood $U_0$ of
$x_0$. For each $y\in U_0$, the derivative matrix
$D_y\Phi(t,y)$ is the solution of the variational equation along $t\mapsto x(t;y)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Fix $(t_0,z_0,\theta_0)\in I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$. Choose a closed time interval and a closed state ball about $(t_0,z_0)$ whose product lies in the open domain; it is compact by [F4]. The continuous function $(t,z)\mapsto\|D_zv(t,z,\theta_0)\|$ is bounded there by [F3]. For each fixed nearby $t$, [F2] on the open state ball gives a state-Lipschitz bound, while smoothness gives continuity of the field. Thus the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses hold locally at every point of the ODE domain.

For each fixed $\theta$ and initial data, [F5] gives the unique local solution and [F6] gives its unique maximal solution on an open interval. Fix now a nonempty compact $K\subseteq\Theta$ and a bounded ball $B$ of initial states. For every $\theta\in K$, the assumptions imply $\|v(t,z,\theta)\|_2\le M_K+L_K\|z\|_2$ on $[0,T]$. For a trajectory starting at $s$ in $B$, its integral equation gives $u(\tau):=\|z(s+\tau)\|_2\le \sup_{x\in B}\|x\|_2+M_K\tau+L_K\int_0^\tau u(\sigma)\,d\sigma$ whenever $s+\tau\in[0,T]$. Apply [F7] with the nondecreasing function $a(\tau)=\sup_{x\in B}\|x\|_2+M_K\tau$; time reversal gives the same bound backward. Thus every such maximal trajectory while it lies in $[0,T]$ has norm at most $R:=(\sup_{x\in B}\|x\|_2+M_KT)e^{L_KT}$. If a right endpoint $\beta$ of its maximal interval belonged to $(s,T]$, the explicitly defined sequence $t_j=\beta-(\beta-s)/(j+1)$ would increase to $\beta$, and each graph point $(t_j,z(t_j))$ would lie in the compact cylinder $[0,T]\times\overline B_R\subset I\times\mathbb R^d$. By [F8] the solution would extend past $\beta$, contradicting maximality. The explicit sequence $t_j=\alpha+(s-\alpha)/(j+1)$ gives the same contradiction at any left endpoint $\alpha\in[0,s)$. Therefore every maximal solution contains all of $[0,T]$, and uniqueness follows from [F6]. The sequences are specified by their endpoint and use no choice axiom.

Fix a base initial state, parameter, and times $s,t$; choose compact neighborhoods $B$ and $K$ of the state and parameter. Step 2.1 places the trajectories for these data in one closed bounded state ball, so $[0,T]\times\overline B_R\times K$ is compact by [F4]. At every point of this cylinder, [F9] and [F10] applied to the smooth augmented field $(z,\theta)'=(v(t,z,\theta),0)$ give an open neighborhood of initial time, state, and parameter, and a positive time radius on which the local transition map is smooth. A finite subcover exists by [F4], and the minimum of its finitely many time radii is positive. Partition the interval from $s$ to $t$ into finitely many segments shorter than this minimum. Each base trajectory node belongs to a selected chart; continuity lets us shrink the initial state and parameter neighborhoods successively so each perturbed node remains in the next chart. The full transition is therefore a finite composition of smooth local maps on a neighborhood of the base data. Since the base data were arbitrary, $(z_s,\theta)\mapsto\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ is locally $C^\infty$ for every fixed $s,t$.

By uniqueness from step 2.1, solving from $s$ to $t$ and then from $t$ back to $s$ returns the original initial value; hence $\Phi^\theta_{s,t}\circ\Phi^\theta_{t,s}$ and $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}\circ\Phi^\theta_{s,t}$ are both identity maps. Both maps are smooth by step 3.1, so each $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}$ is a global $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism with the stated inverse.

Fix $s,\theta,z_s$. At every interior time $r\in(0,T)$, smoothness of the field and [F10] give a common local interval for nearby initial states at $z_r:=\Phi^\theta_{r,s}(z_s)$. The hypotheses of [F11] hold there, so $A(t):=D_y\Phi^\theta_{t,r}(z_r)$ satisfies $A'(r)=D_zv(r,z_r,\theta)$ and $A(r)=I_d$. Uniqueness gives $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}=\Phi^\theta_{t,r}\circ\Phi^\theta_{r,s}$ near $t=r$; differentiating this identity in $z_s$ using [F12] yields $J_{t,s}=A(t)J_{r,s}$. Differentiating at $t=r$ therefore gives $\frac{d}{dt}J_{t,s}=D_zv(r,\Phi^\theta_{r,s}(z_s),\theta)J_{r,s}$. Since $r$ was arbitrary this holds on $(0,T)$; the local transitions at $0,T$ give the corresponding one-sided derivatives. At $t=s$, the transition is the identity and so $J_{s,s}=I_d$.

Let $T>0$, let $d,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly $C^\infty$. For every compact $K\subseteq\Theta$, suppose there are constants $L_K,M_K\ge0$ such that, for all $t\in[0,T]$, $\theta\in K$, and $z,w\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|v(t,z,\theta)-v(t,w,\theta)\|_2\le L_K\|z-w\|_2,\qquad \|v(t,0,\theta)\|_2\le M_K.$$

Then for each $\theta\in\Theta$, $s,t\in[0,T]$, and $z_s\in\mathbb R^d$, the neural ODE has a unique solution on all of $[0,T]$. Write $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ for its value at time $t$. For each fixed $s,t$, the map $(z_s,\theta)\mapsto\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ is locally $C^\infty$. For each fixed $\theta$, $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi^\theta_{s,t}$. Its state Jacobian $J_{t,s}:=D_{z_s}\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}J_{t,s}=D_zv(t,\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s),\theta)J_{t,s},\qquad J_{s,s}=I_d.$$

Time derivatives at $0$ and $T$ are one-sided.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $U_0\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $T>0$, and let $f$ be jointly $C^1$ on an open time-state domain. Suppose the ODE $x'(t)=f(t,x(t))$ has a common flow
$$\Phi:[0,T]\times U_0\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad x(t)=\Phi_t(x_0),$$
whose time slices $\Phi_t:U_0\to U_t$ are $C^1$ diffeomorphisms onto open sets $U_t$, with $\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}_{U_0}$. Let $p_0:U_0\to(0,\infty)$ be a continuous probability density with respect to Lebesgue measure, let $\mu_t$ be the pushforward of $p_0(x)\,dx$ under $\Phi_t$, and define
$$p_t(y):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{p_0(\Phi_t^{-1}(y))}{|\det D\Phi_t(\Phi_t^{-1}(y))|},&y\in U_t,\\0,&y\notin U_t.\end{cases}$$
Then $p_t$ is a density of $\mu_t$ on $\mathbb R^d$, the flow Jacobian has positive determinant, and
$$p_t(\Phi_t(x_0))=\frac{p_0(x_0)}{\det D\Phi_t(x_0)}>0,$$
and, for $0<t<T$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\log p_t(x(t))=-\operatorname{div}_x f(t,x(t)),\qquad \operatorname{div}_x f:=\operatorname{tr}D_xf=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{x_i}f_i.$$
The derivative at $0$ or $T$ is understood one-sided.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$. By [F1] this is a first-order IVP, and [F2] supplies its flow $\Phi_t$ on all of $[0,T]$; every slice is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$ and $\Phi_0$ is the identity. Hence the flow and initial density satisfy the hypotheses of [F3].

Apply [F3] using the assumed Countable Choice [A1]. It gives that the displayed $p_t$ is a density of the pushforward and that $p_t(\Phi_t(z_0))=p_0(z_0)/\det J_t>0$ with logarithmic derivative $-\operatorname{tr}(D_zv(t,z_t,\theta))$. By the definition of trace as the sum of diagonal entries, this is $-\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{z_i}v_i(t,z_t,\theta)$; [F3] gives the stated endpoint convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\Theta$ be open with compact closure contained in $\Theta$, let $U_0\subseteq\Theta$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and let $u_0:U_0\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Write $u_\theta$ for the exact solution of $\dot u_\theta(t)=v(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$, $u_\theta(0)=u_0(\theta)$, and let $\mathcal T:=\{(t,u_\theta(t),\theta):t\in[0,T],\theta\in\overline\Omega\}$ be its common compact trajectory tube. Let

$$\mathcal T_T:=\{(u_\theta(T),\theta):\theta\in\overline\Omega\}$$

be the terminal state-parameter slice. Let $U_\phi\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ and $U_\ell\subseteq I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open sets containing $\mathcal T_T$ and $\mathcal T$, respectively, and let $\phi:U_\phi\to\mathbb R$ and $\ell:U_\ell\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Assume their first derivatives, measured in Euclidean operator norms, are bounded and uniformly continuous on $\mathcal T_T$ and $\mathcal T$, respectively. Define

$$\mathcal J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt.$$

For each $\theta\in\Omega$, the exact continuous adjoint sensitivity procedure is:

1. Solve the state initial-value problem forward on $[0,T]$.
2. Solve the terminal adjoint problem backward,
   $$-p'(t)=D_u v(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T p(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
3. Return the vector
   $$G(\theta)=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\left(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T+D_\theta v(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)\right)dt.$$

Here $D_u$ and $D_\theta$ denote Jacobian matrices in the displayed variables, $p(t)\in\mathbb R^d$, and $G(\theta)\in\mathbb R^q$. All state and adjoint equations and the integral are exact continuous mathematical objects. Replacing them by numerical solver outputs defines a finite computation and is outside this algorithm's accuracy guarantees.

Assume $T>0$. Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

derivations.claim: By [F7, F8, F10], $u_1(t)=\exp(-t)$ and $u_2(t)=\exp(\theta t)$ satisfy the displayed ODE and initial data. By [F2] this is the unique flow, so $\mathcal J(\theta)=\exp(\theta)$ and $\mathcal J'(-100)=\exp(-100)$.

The Euler transition is the C1 map $\Psi_k(u,\theta)=((1-1/N)u_1,(1+\theta/N)u_2)$. It is a finite state-step objective as in [F5], and induction gives $u_{2,N}=(1+\theta/N)^N$. By [F10], differentiating this polynomial gives $(1+\theta/N)^{N-1}$; by [F6], the finite discrete adjoint returns exactly this derivative.

For the continuous adjoint, $D_u v=\operatorname{diag}(-1,\theta)$, $p(1)=(0,1)$, and $p(t)=(0,\exp(\theta(1-t)))$ solves the terminal adjoint equation by [F8, F10]. Substituting into [F4] gives $\int_0^1\exp(\theta t)\exp(\theta(1-t))\,dt=\int_0^1\exp(\theta)\,dt=\exp(\theta)$ by [F11], which is also the output expression defined by [F3].

At $\theta=-100$, $N=50$ gives $(1-2)^{49}=-1$, while $N=100$ gives $(1-1)^{99}=0$. By [F9], $\exp(-100)>0$, so both finite gradients differ from the exact continuous gradient; the two finite gradients also differ from each other. This establishes only the stated finite witness, not a general error bound.
